latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Active replication of influenza A/B in respiratory epithelium; drives early symptoms, fever, contagiousness, and is the direct target of NA inhibitors and baloxavir.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Innate antiviral type I interferon response
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Host IFN-alpha/beta response that simultaneously controls viral replication and produces classic flu-like symptoms (myalgia, headache, malaise, fever).
IL-6/TNF/IL-1-mediated acute phase response producing high fever, rigors, myalgia, anorexia, neutrophil shifts, and CRP elevation.
Direct viral lysis of ciliated columnar epithelium; underlies dry cough, retrosternal soreness, mucociliary clearance failure, and predisposes to secondary bacterial colonization.
Diffuse alveolar damage from direct viral infection of pneumocytes; drives hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrates, and ARDS, especially in pregnancy, H1N1, H5/H7 strains.

S. pneumoniae, S. aureus (incl. MRSA), H. influenzae, GAS superinfection of damaged respiratory epithelium; classically biphasic course with secondary fever and consolidation after initial improvement.
Inflammatory bronchitis with bronchospasm; drives prolonged cough, asthma/COPD exacerbation, and post-viral airway hyperresponsiveness lasting weeks.
Direct viral and immune-mediated skeletal muscle injury; classically calf myositis in children (influenza B > A), occasionally rhabdomyolysis with CK elevation and AKI.
Direct viral and cytokine-mediated myocardial inflammation; can present as fulminant myocarditis with troponin elevation, LV dysfunction, arrhythmia, and cardiogenic shock.
Pediatric-predominant cytokine-mediated encephalopathy with thalamic/brainstem necrosis; rapid coma, seizures, high mortality. Adult encephalitis less common but recognized.
Influenza as a major trigger of asthma and COPD exacerbations via airway inflammation and bronchospasm; drives wheeze, dyspnea, hypoxia, and need for systemic steroids/bronchodilators.
Prolonged fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance after acute resolution, lasting 1-4 weeks beyond viral clearance.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Viral PAMPs (ssRNA via TLR7, RIG-I) trigger type I IFN production proportional to viral load.
Influenza is directly cytopathic to ciliated airway epithelium; injury scales with viral burden.
Type I IFN signaling drives downstream IL-6/TNF/IL-1 and acute phase response.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: high viral burden, virulent strain (H1N1pdm, H5N1, H7N9), or impaired host immunity
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Distal alveolar viral replication produces diffuse alveolar damage and viral pneumonia.
Loss of ciliated epithelium and impaired mucociliary clearance + IFN-induced AM dysfunction enable bacterial superinfection (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae).
Tracheobronchial epithelial injury produces airway inflammation, hyperreactivity, and prolonged cough.
Viral airway inflammation triggers bronchospasm and acute exacerbation in obstructive airway disease.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: more common in influenza B, especially in children
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Direct viral and immune-mediated muscle fiber injury; influenza B benign acute childhood myositis classically affects calves.
Direct viral invasion of myocardium plus cytokine-mediated injury produces myocarditis with troponin release and LV dysfunction.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: predominantly pediatric; rare in adults; East Asian genetic susceptibility (RANBP2 in ANE1)
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Hypercytokinemia (IL-6, TNF, IL-1) drives BBB disruption and thalamic/brainstem necrosis; viremia is typically absent.
IL-1/IL-6/IFN-driven hypothalamic set-point elevation produces high fever 38.5-40°C, often with abrupt onset and rigor.
Acute phase pyrogenic cytokines drive fever; fever curve tracks cytokine activity.
Abrupt rise in thermoregulatory set-point produces shaking chills, characteristic of influenza onset.
Type I IFN is a major driver of diffuse myalgia, the cardinal flu symptom.
IFN signaling and prostaglandin pathways produce frontal/retro-orbital headache.
Sickness behavior driven by IFN/cytokine signaling produces profound prostration and fatigue.
Tracheobronchial inflammation produces dry, often painful cough; characteristic of influenza.
Airway hyperreactivity produces prolonged post-influenza cough often lasting 2-3 weeks.
Pharyngeal mucosal inflammation produces sore throat; usually less prominent than in streptococcal pharyngitis.
IL-6-driven hepatic acute phase response; CRP typically modest in uncomplicated flu (10-80 mg/L), markedly elevated when bacterial superinfection or pneumonia complicates.
Bacterial superinfection drives marked CRP elevation (often >100 mg/L), distinguishing from uncomplicated viral course.
Procalcitonin rises with bacterial superinfection; uncomplicated influenza typically keeps PCT low (<0.25 ng/mL), making PCT useful for ruling in superinfection.
Lymphopenia is characteristic of influenza, driven by lymphocyte redistribution and apoptosis.
Mild leukopenia or normal WBC is characteristic of uncomplicated influenza; marked leukocytosis suggests bacterial complication.
Bacterial superinfection drives neutrophilic leukocytosis with left shift.
Mild thrombocytopenia common in severe influenza, especially with H5N1, H1N1pdm, or with HLH/secondary HLH complication.
RT-PCR sensitivity highest during peak viral shedding (days 1-4); remains positive longer than rapid antigen.
Rapid antigen detection requires high viral load; sensitivity ~50-70%, peaks days 1-3, drops sharply after day 4.
Primary viral pneumonia produces bilateral interstitial/ground-glass infiltrates, often peripheral, can progress to ARDS pattern.
Bacterial superinfection produces lobar or focal alveolar consolidation, often with new infiltrate after initial improvement.
Diffuse alveolar damage produces V/Q mismatch and shunt physiology.
Lobar consolidation reduces gas exchange surface.
Hypoxemia and increased work of breathing drive tachypnea; key bedside marker of severity.
Fever and inflammatory state drive sinus tachycardia.
Skeletal muscle injury releases CK; mild elevation common, marked elevation (>5000 U/L) defines rhabdomyolysis.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: calf-predominant in pediatric influenza B benign acute childhood myositis
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Direct muscle inflammation produces focal calf tenderness and refusal to walk in children.
Myocyte injury releases troponin; degree of elevation correlates with severity of myocarditis.
Myocardial inflammation and concomitant pericarditis produce pleuritic or ischemic-quality chest pain.
Cytokine-mediated CNS injury produces rapid altered consciousness, often progressing to coma.
Cortical and thalamic involvement produces seizures, often early in encephalopathy course.
Severe viral pneumonia is the dominant pathway to ARDS in influenza, especially with H1N1pdm and pregnancy.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: S. aureus (especially MRSA, PVL+) necrotizing pneumonia is a high-mortality phenotype
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Bacterial superinfection, especially S. aureus, is a leading cause of post-influenza ARDS and mortality.
Direct activity to clinical myocarditis event hazard.
Myoglobinuric AKI from severe rhabdomyolysis.
Primary viral pneumonia with respiratory failure is a major mortality pathway, especially in pregnant women, elderly, and immunocompromised.
Post-influenza S. aureus and pneumococcal pneumonia historically account for a large fraction of influenza mortality (1918 pandemic, ongoing seasonal).
Fulminant myocarditis causes cardiogenic shock and arrhythmic death.
Acute necrotizing encephalopathy carries high mortality.
Severe COPD/asthma exacerbations can produce respiratory failure and death.

axes.shape_free_text: Abrupt onset 38.5-40°C (often >39°C) within 24 h, sustained 2-4 days, defervescence by day 5-7. Biphasic fever (return after defervescence) suggests bacterial superinfection.
axes.second_peak: biphasic recurrence on day 5-14 strongly suggests secondary bacterial pneumonia

axes.shape_free_text: Patient-reported or documented fever history when an exact temperature is not available; abrupt fever is one of the core influenza presentation anchors.
Sinus tachycardia tracking fever, typically 90-120 bpm; resolves with defervescence.
Normal 12-20 in uncomplicated flu; tachypnea >24 indicates pneumonia or ARDS, and fulminant primary viral pneumonia can drive respiratory rates into the 40-50/min range.
Normal in uncomplicated flu; drop to <94% suggests viral or bacterial pneumonia, and primary influenza viral pneumonia/ARDS can produce profound room-air hypoxemia.
Preserved in uncomplicated influenza; falls in primary viral pneumonia or ARDS. This captures oxygenation severity when ABG and FiO2 are available.
Usually preserved; hypotension only in severe pneumonia, myocarditis, septic shock, or rhabdomyolysis-driven volume depletion.
Normal or mildly low (3-7) in uncomplicated influenza; marked leukocytosis (>12) suggests bacterial superinfection.
Lymphopenia is characteristic, often 0.5-1.2; recovery with viral clearance.
Variable; usually normal in uncomplicated flu; neutrophilia with left shift in bacterial superinfection.
Normal or mildly decreased in uncomplicated flu; severe thrombocytopenia in HLH, DIC, or severe H5N1/H1N1pdm.
Modestly elevated in uncomplicated flu (10-80 mg/L); markedly elevated (>100 mg/L) suggests bacterial superinfection or severe pneumonia.
axes.second_peak: secondary rise after defervescence suggests bacterial superinfection

axes.shape_free_text: Typically low (<0.25) in uncomplicated viral influenza; rise above 0.5 raises suspicion for bacterial superinfection.
Mild-moderate elevation in viral pneumonia, severe in primary viral pneumonia/ARDS or HLH complication.
Mild transaminitis common in moderate-severe influenza; marked elevation in HLH or severe systemic disease.
Mild transaminitis; AST disproportionately elevated when myositis/rhabdomyolysis present (CK source).
Mild elevation in many adults; marked elevation (>5000) defines rhabdomyolysis, especially with influenza B in children and severe adult disease.
Usually normal; rises with rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI, severe sepsis, or pre-existing CKD.
Normal in uncomplicated flu; elevated in influenza myocarditis, can mimic ACS.
Cardinal symptom; dry cough at onset, may become productive with airway inflammation; can persist 2-3 weeks after fever resolves.
Absent or mild in uncomplicated influenza; prominent dyspnea indicates viral pneumonia, bacterial superinfection, asthma/COPD exacerbation, myocarditis, or ARDS.
Common but usually less prominent than streptococcal pharyngitis; resolves 5-7 days.
Cardinal flu symptom; diffuse, often severe, peaks early. Calf-predominant in pediatric influenza B myositis.
Cardinal early symptom; frontal/retro-orbital, often severe.
Profound prostration in acute phase; lingering fatigue 1-4 weeks after viral resolution.
Shaking chills at onset, characteristic of influenza fever rise.
Retrosternal soreness from tracheitis common; pleuritic or ischemic-quality chest pain raises suspicion for pneumonia or myocarditis.
Normal in uncomplicated flu; altered mental status raises concern for influenza-associated encephalopathy (especially pediatric), severe sepsis, or hypoxia.
Febrile seizures in young children; new seizure activity in adults raises concern for encephalopathy/encephalitis.
RT-PCR (NP swab or lower respiratory) positive during acute viral shedding, days 1-5; sensitivity 90-95%. Lower respiratory specimens preferred in severe pneumonia even with negative upper sample.
Rapid antigen sensitivity 50-70%, peaks days 1-3, drops sharply after day 4. Negative result does not exclude influenza.

Influenza A (H1N1pdm09, H3N2) vs B vs novel zoonotic (H5N1, H7N9, H5N6). H3N2 worse in elderly; H1N1pdm09 worse in pregnancy/young adults; B associated with childhood myositis; novel avian have markedly higher mortality.
H275Y mutation produces oseltamivir resistance; rare in seasonal H1N1pdm09 but can emerge in immunocompromised on prolonged therapy.
PA I38T/F/M substitution produces baloxavir resistance, can emerge during treatment, especially in children.
Time-from-symptom-onset to NA inhibitor initiation; benefit greatest within 48 h, declines but may persist in severe/hospitalized cases.
Chest imaging extent of consolidation/infiltrate; absent in uncomplicated flu, focal in bacterial superinfection, diffuse bilateral in primary viral pneumonia/ARDS.
Bilateral peripheral ground-glass/interstitial pattern, may progress to diffuse alveolar damage and ARDS pattern.
Most common: S. pneumoniae > S. aureus (incl. MRSA, often necrotizing/cavitary) > H. influenzae > GAS. S. aureus post-influenza pneumonia carries high mortality.
Probability that respiratory tract is the active infectious source - always near 1 in influenza.
Low in uncomplicated flu; markedly elevated with primary viral pneumonia (esp. H1N1pdm in pregnancy) or severe S. aureus superinfection.
Rare; elevated days 3-10, can present as fulminant cardiogenic shock.
Elevated in severe influenza, mainly via rhabdomyolysis, sepsis, or volume depletion.
Elevated days 5-14 due to airway epithelial injury and IFN-induced macrophage dysfunction; biphasic clinical course is the hallmark.
Rare overall; elevated in young children, especially East Asian populations (RANBP2 ANE1).

Very low in uncomplicated outpatient flu (~0.1% case fatality); rises 10-100x with viral pneumonia, bacterial superinfection, myocarditis, encephalopathy, in elderly, pregnant, or immunocompromised hosts.
Current-season vaccination protection; lowers severity and mortality even when infection occurs (breakthrough).

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Sinus tachycardia tracks fever (~10 bpm per 1°C). Disproportionate tachycardia raises concern for myocarditis, dehydration, or pneumonia.
Bacterial superinfection event drives biphasic fever pattern after initial defervescence.
Tachypnea in pneumonia/ARDS reflects compensation for hypoxemia.
Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis drives AKI with creatinine rise.
Both rise with bacterial superinfection but PCT rises more selectively.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Symptomatic benefit and viral shedding reduction strongest when started within 48 h; outpatient mortality benefit largely confined to early initiation.
H275Y mutation confers high-level oseltamivir resistance; switch to baloxavir or zanamivir.
Renally cleared - dose reduce in CrCl <60 mL/min.

failure_modes: delayed initiation beyond 48-72 h reduces benefit
severe disease may still progress despite therapy

side_effects.interpretation: GI upset (nausea, vomiting) common but usually mild

treatments.context_specific_role: First-line definitive antiviral; oral, suitable for outpatient and inpatient. Standard 5-day course (75 mg BID adult); longer courses in severe/immunocompromised disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: PA I38T substitution emerges during/after baloxavir treatment, especially in children, reduces effect.

failure_modes: post-treatment emergence of PA I38 mutation
limited evidence for severe hospitalized influenza compared to oseltamivir
treatments.context_specific_role: Single-dose oral antiviral, simple compliance. Used for uncomplicated influenza in outpatients; alternative when oseltamivir resistance suspected. Less established for severe inpatient disease.

failure_modes: limited oral intake patients require IV but evidence base smaller
shared NA inhibitor resistance with oseltamivir
treatments.context_specific_role: IV NA inhibitor (single dose); useful when oral route unavailable or inadequate (severe nausea, intubated patients).

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Inhaled lactose-based powder can precipitate bronchospasm; contraindicated in asthma/COPD.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative NA inhibitor when oseltamivir resistance suspected; avoid in obstructive airway disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Empiric antibacterials only beneficial when bacterial superinfection present; should cover S. aureus (incl. MRSA) and S. pneumoniae in severe post-influenza pneumonia.
Low PCT supports viral-only process and may guide antibiotic de-escalation.

failure_modes: uncomplicated viral influenza without bacterial superinfection - antibiotic exposure without benefit
MRSA not covered by standard CAP regimens
necrotizing S. aureus pneumonia may need toxin-suppressing agents (linezolid/clindamycin)

side_effects.interpretation: C. difficile risk with broad-spectrum antibiotics

treatments.context_specific_role: Add to antiviral when severe pneumonia with bacterial superinfection suspected (focal/lobar consolidation, biphasic fever, marked CRP/PCT rise, leukocytosis with left shift). MRSA coverage critical given necrotizing S. aureus post-influenza pneumonia.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe primary viral pneumonia requires oxygen, HFNC, NIV, or mechanical ventilation; lung-protective ventilation in ARDS.

failure_modes: refractory hypoxemia despite mechanical ventilation may require ECMO (selected centers)
treatments.context_specific_role: Cornerstone for hypoxemic respiratory failure; lung-protective strategy for ARDS; ECMO consideration in refractory cases.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pre-exposure protection; reduces disease incidence (40-60%) and severity even with breakthrough infection.

failure_modes: lower effectiveness in elderly and immunocompromised
treatments.context_specific_role: Annual prevention; not a treatment for active disease but central to disease ecology and outcome modulation. High priority in elderly, pregnant, healthcare workers, chronic disease.

high.trajectory_modulation: Higher mortality, more secondary bacterial pneumonia, more cardiovascular complications. H3N2 seasons disproportionately affect elderly.
Higher rates of febrile seizures, encephalopathy (especially East Asian populations), benign acute childhood myositis (influenza B), hospitalization.

present.trajectory_modulation: Markedly increased risk of severe primary viral pneumonia, ARDS, ICU admission, and mortality, especially with H1N1pdm09. Vaccination and early oseltamivir strongly indicated.
Acute exacerbation common; need for systemic steroids, bronchodilators; respiratory failure risk elevated.
Increased risk of acute MI, decompensated heart failure, and arrhythmia in 1-2 weeks following influenza; significant cardiovascular mortality contribution.
Hospitalization and mortality elevated; metabolic decompensation (DKA, HHS) during acute illness.
Identified during H1N1pdm09 pandemic as independent risk factor for severe disease, ICU admission, mortality.
Prolonged viral shedding, higher resistance emergence (NA inhibitor or baloxavir), more severe pneumonia, atypical/protracted course; longer/higher-dose antiviral courses indicated.
Higher mortality; oseltamivir requires dose adjustment in renal impairment.
Impaired airway clearance; increased pneumonia and mortality risk.
Reduced incidence and severity of breakthrough infection.
Strong susceptibility to acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE1) - a recognized severe pediatric phenotype.
Zoonotic strains (H5N1, H7N9, H5N6) carry markedly higher case fatality (30-60%) with severe primary viral pneumonia.

supportive_care: antipyretics (acetaminophen preferred; avoid aspirin in children due to Reye syndrome risk)
oral hydration; IV fluids for severe disease or volume depletion
rest and isolation (droplet precautions, 7 days from symptom onset or until afebrile 24 h, longer in immunocompromised)
supplemental oxygen titrated to SpO2 ≥94% (lower target in COPD)
high-flow nasal cannula or non-invasive ventilation in moderate hypoxemic respiratory failure
lung-protective mechanical ventilation (low tidal volume, prone positioning) for ARDS
ECMO consideration in refractory ARDS at experienced centers
bronchodilators and short-course systemic corticosteroids for asthma/COPD exacerbation
avoid routine systemic corticosteroids for influenza pneumonia alone (associated with worse outcomes unless indicated for ARDS, septic shock, or asthma/COPD exacerbation)
deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis in hospitalized patients
early empiric broad-spectrum antibacterials with anti-MRSA coverage when secondary bacterial pneumonia suspected (biphasic fever, focal infiltrate, leukocytosis, elevated procalcitonin)
blood cultures and respiratory cultures before antibiotics in severe disease
echocardiography and troponin/ECG if myocarditis suspected
neuroimaging and EEG if encephalopathy suspected; IVIG/steroids in selected pediatric ANE
post-exposure prophylaxis with oseltamivir for high-risk household contacts during outbreaks
annual seasonal influenza vaccination for prevention, especially in elderly, pregnant, healthcare workers, and chronic disease patients
infection control: droplet precautions, hand hygiene, masking of symptomatic individuals
